newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina mulls how many retirees owed court award.
newsitem.headline: Argentina mulls how many retirees owed court award.

text.p: The Argentine government is studying whether a court-awarded increase of nearly 14 percent in back payments to 70,000 pensioners in fact applies to thousands more, an official said Thursday.

Deputy Labor Minister Carlos Torres, who heads the ANSeS social security department, said in comments reported by local news agency DyN that he expects results in the next few days of a study of last Friday's Supreme Court decision.
"We are evaluating the ruling to see what implications it has for the rest of the pensioners," said Torres.
He said that while the ruling only referred to 70,000 pensioners, it will automatically benefit all 125,000 pensioners suing for an increase.

But it could potentially apply to many more. Argentina has about three million state pensioners. Nearly one million retired after 1991 and their payments cannot be affected by the court ruling, while another half million are on so-called "special regime" pensions linked to the movements of wages in the sectors where they worked.

The Clarin newspaper reported Thursday that this means only half the three million state pensioners could seek an increase in back payments in line with the 13.8 percent rise. The newspaper calculated that would cost the state $800 million a year.
The Argentine government has yet to issue a calculation of the cost of last Friday's Supreme Court ruling retroactively granting pensioners a 13.8 percent increase for 1991 to 1994.
The economic stability plan launched by the Peronist government in 1991, which pegged the peso to the dollar, ended automatic adjustments to pensions to compensate for inflation.
Economy Ministry officials said earlier this week the backdated payments would be financed with existing bonds and new bond issues.
